claim.quote: Detection of the Free Neutrino: a Confirmation

date.note: First public presentation of the result, month precision. The Science paper followed on 20 July 1956; Reines and Cowan telegrammed Pauli the same month.
date.quote: The results of the present work were presented in a Post deadline paper, American Physical Society, New Haven Meeting, June, 1956.

key_value_text.quote: In one set of runs, the neutrino signal rate was 0.56 ± 0.06 count per hour, and with changed requirements it was 2.88 ± 0.22 counts per hour.
key_value_text.value: Reactor-power-dependent neutrino signal of 0.56 ± 0.06 counts per hour (2.88 ± 0.22 with changed requirements), against an accidental background about 20 times smaller

name: Detection of the Free Neutrino: a Confirmation
notes: Classified first_detection because the paper title says "Detection" and the APS plaque says "first experiment that conclusively detected the neutrino"; the paper itself calls its own result a confirmation of the Hanford 1953 tentative identification.
date is the June 1956 APS meeting presentation (month precision); the day-precision publication date is in `published`.

published.note: Issue date of the Science paper.

summary.plain: Cowan and Reines reported at the June 1956 APS meeting, and in Science on 20 July 1956, that a reactor-power-dependent signal in their tank detector matched the reaction antineutrino + proton -> positron + neutron, so the neutrino exists. The paper calls it a confirmation of a 1953 tentative identification at Hanford.
summary.technical: Delayed-coincidence signal with the reactor-power dependence, proton-density, shielding and cadmium tests expected of reactor antineutrinos: 0.56 ± 0.06 counts per hour (2.88 ± 0.22 with changed requirements) in 1371 h of running, a cross section within 5% of 6.3×10⁻⁴⁴ cm² against a prediction uncertain by ±25%.

title: Detection of the Free Neutrino: a Confirmation
why_it_matters: The American Physical Society's 2014 Savannah River plaque calls it "the first experiment that conclusively detected the neutrino", and the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics gave Frederick Reines one half "for the detection of the neutrino".
